summary: RFC 7589 protects NETCONF messages with TLS 1.2. This document updates it with revised TLS 1.2 support requirements and TLS 1.3 requirements, including limits on TLS 1.3 early data.

eli5.summary: The sealed envelope around network management messages gets upgraded to the newest kind, with a rule against sending sensitive stuff too early.

questions: does netconf over tls support tls 1.3
is early data allowed in netconf over tls
what port does netconf over tls use
subtitle: Updated TLS rules for NETCONF: TLS 1.2 stays mandatory, TLS 1.3 is added, and early data is banned.

tldr.problem: RFC 7589 protects NETCONF messages with TLS 1.2 only, so it has no requirements for TLS 1.3 and says nothing about TLS 1.3 early data.
tldr.mechanism: This document updates the support requirements for TLS 1.2, adds support requirements for TLS 1.3, and says NETCONF implementations that support TLS 1.3 or later MUST NOT use early data.
tldr.outcome: Implementations MUST support mutually authenticated TLS 1.2 and SHOULD support TLS 1.3, preferring it when implemented. The IANA entry for netconf-tls now also points to this document.

facts.label: TLS 1.3
facts.value: SHOULD support; MUST prefer if implemented

today: RFC 9918 is a Proposed Standard published in July 2026. It updates RFC 7589 and has not been updated or obsoleted itself.

sections.title: What This Update Changes
sections.content:
RFC 7589 defines how to protect NETCONF messages with TLS 1.2. This document updates it in three ways: it updates the support requirements for TLS 1.2, it adds TLS 1.3 support requirements including limits on early data, and it updates the IANA-registered netconf-tls port entry to refer to this document.

All other provisions of RFC 7589 are unchanged, including connection initiation, message framing, connection closure, certificate validation, server identity and client identity. Implementations that support TLS 1.3 SHOULD also follow Sections 4 and 5 of RFC 7589.
sections.eli5: There was already a rulebook for locking network management messages in a safe. This note adds rules for the newer kind of lock and leaves the rest alone.

sections.title: Early Data Is Not Allowed
sections.content:
Early data, also called 0-RTT data, is a TLS 1.3 mechanism that lets a client send data in the first flight of messages to a server. It is permitted only when client and server share a Pre-Shared Key (PSK). TLS 1.3 can be used without it.

The security properties of early data are weaker than those of later TLS-protected data. It is not forward secret, and there is no protection against replay of early data between connections. This document therefore specifies that NETCONF implementations that support TLS 1.3 or later MUST NOT use early data.
sections.eli5: Sending your message before the secret handshake is finished is risky, because someone could copy it and send it again. NETCONF is not allowed to do that.

sections.title: TLS Versions and Cipher Suites
sections.content:
Implementations MUST support mutually authenticated TLS 1.2 and are recommended to support the cipher suites in Section 4.2 of RFC 9325. They MAY implement additional TLS 1.2 cipher suites that provide mutual authentication and confidentiality.

Implementations SHOULD support mutually authenticated TLS 1.3 and, if they implement it, MUST prefer to negotiate TLS 1.3 over earlier versions. Those that support TLS 1.3 are REQUIRED to support the mandatory-to-implement cipher suites in Section 9.1 of RFC 9846, and MAY implement additional suites that provide mutual authentication and confidentiality.

NETCONF over TLS still requires mutual authentication, so neither side should connect to an unknown, unexpected or incorrectly identified peer. Where a trusted list of CA certificates is used, the listed CAs should only issue certificates to parties authorized to access the NETCONF servers.
sections.eli5: The older lock must always work, the newer lock is strongly encouraged, and if both sides have the newer lock they should use it. Both sides must also show ID to each other.

sections.title: The netconf-tls Registry Entry
sections.content: IANA added a reference to this document in the netconf-tls entry of the Service Name and Transport Protocol Port Number Registry. The entry is for port 6513 over tcp, described as NETCONF over TLS, and its reference now reads RFC 7589, RFC 9918.
sections.eli5: The phone book entry for this service now lists this note too, but the phone number did not change.
